As telecom operators move toward cloud-native networks, BCG’s analysis of voice-service infrastructure shows that shared, managed core network services can accelerate launches and cut costs. The choice is not whether to modernize, but which capabilities should remain in-house and which should be standardized.

Shared services work best where networks offer little differentiationCore network as a service suits standardized functions such as voice, Internet of Things, and roaming, where reliability and compliance matter more than customized features.

A managed voice platform speeds commercial launchMoving from traditional voice infrastructure to cloud-native deployment cuts readiness time by roughly 50%; a shared managed model removes another 30% through pre-integrated designs and reusable testing.

Cost benefits are strongest for smaller operatorsFor a network serving 1 million subscribers, managed cloud-native voice can lower five-year per-subscriber ownership costs by 50% versus operator-run cloud infrastructure and 80% versus legacy systems.

Scale and control still justify in-house deployment in some casesAt 5 million subscribers, the managed model’s cost advantage falls to about 10%. Large operators may retain dedicated platforms when customization, sovereignty, regulation, or established scale require direct control.

For telco operators of all sizes, one of the most important strategic questions is how to build out the network to compete with new commercial ideas, enter frontier markets, and serve existing ones more cost effectively. In a 2025 article, we highlighted why transitioning to cloud-native architectures—characterized by modular, containerized microservices, automated orchestration and life-cycle management, and the ability to scale individual functions up and down on standardized infrastructure—is integral to future telco networks.We now see the first wave of operators exploring core network as a service (CNaaS), which takes this transformation a step further by industrializing delivery, shifting from individually deployed and operated core network functions toward standardized, shared services. CNaaS can range from individual functions, such as the IP multimedia subsystem (IMS), to dedicated Internet of Things (IoT) cores and full mobile cores.In a compelling case study involving IMS, the platform for delivering voice services over 4G/5G networks, we found that cloud-native IMS offers two major benefits. It can significantly reduce the time to commercial readiness, and it can lower the total cost of ownership (TCO) compared with traditional IMS. We also found that applying CNaaS principles can add to those benefits.Looking forward, this case study offers a path for adding other standardized network services. For small and medium-size operators, these services include private enterprise networks, IoT and non-terrestrial network (NTN) use cases, roaming enablement, and Network API Gateway-as-a-Service. For larger operators, they include contained use cases where initial scale or market uptake does not yet justify dedicated platform and operating capabilities.CNaaS Changes the Operating Model
Under an operator-deployed cloud solution, the operator retains responsibility for platform build and integration, infrastructure, monitoring, upgrades, specialist operations, and life-cycle management. CNaaS builds on cloud-native architecture, allowing CNaaS providers to package common infrastructure and carrier-grade platform capabilities—such as security, observability, automation and resilience—into a standardized, pre-integrated, reusable telco cloud, rather than engineered separately for each operator’s deployment.With more of these responsibilities included in the managed service, the operator can focus on network integration, service management, regulatory requirements, and migration. Successfully launching a shared network function requires the operator and the CNaaS provider to agree upfront on clear governance, covering roadmap prioritization, upgrade scheduling, and change approval. The operator and the CNaaS provider also need to establish clearly defined responsibilities, joint ways of working for onboarding, rules for incident and release management, and service-level agreements that reflect carrier-grade requirements.By sharing infrastructure, platform engineering, and specialist operations across deployments via a CNaaS model, operators can spread fixed costs and scarce cloud-native telecom expertise. Together, these elements provide a repeatable foundation for deploying standardized network services across markets and operators.Determining Where CNaaS Works Best
To assess whether a service is better suited to the CNaaS model or to the operator-deployed cloud model, we developed BCG’s CNaaS attractiveness framework. (See Exhibit 1.) This framework evaluates each service or use case along two dimensions: the degree of service standardization and reuse potential, and the potential scale of the service or market assessed in association with the operator's internal capabilities to deploy and operate it independently.

The strongest CNaaS fit typically arises in settings involving standardized services, limited differentiation, and a level of service-specific scale or internal capabilities that do not justify dedicated platform and operating resources. Some companies that initially focused on mobile virtual network operators (MVNO) and IoT platforms are now expanding into IMS and 5G standalone packet core networks. These examples illustrate how CNaaS can support both specialized core network functions and broader mobile services without requiring each customer to build and operate dedicated infrastructure.

IMS Is an Ideal Case Study
Our framework indicates that IMS is a sweet spot for CNaaS and makes IMSaaS an ideal case study. IMS supports essential, carrier-grade native voice services that are highly standardized and offer limited scope for competitive differentiation. For this reason, reliability, regulatory compliance, low cost, and operational simplicity are the primary requirements.Both operator-deployed cloud-native IMS and IMSaaS benefit from their cloud-native foundation, which improves planning, deployment, and operations compared with traditional IMS. IMSaaS adds a second layer of benefits through CNaaS industrialization, including standardized service designs, reusable integration assets, and shared operational capabilities. (See Exhibit 2.)

To separate the benefits of a cloud-native architecture from those of the IMSaaS model, our analysis compares commercial readiness and TCO for three IMS models:Traditional IMS. In this model, operator-owned IMS runs on vendor-specific hardware or virtual network functions in a non-cloud-native stack.Operator-deployed cloud-native IMS. This model entails deploying cloud-native IMS on infrastructure controlled by the operator, which retains responsibility for platform build and integration, operations, and life-cycle management.IMSaaS. Here, the CNaaS provider delivers a standardized, pre-integrated managed service on a telco cloud. The model combines reusable integration capabilities, shared specialist expertise and operations, and centrally managed life-cycle activities.Time to Commercial Readiness Improves
IMSaaS can accelerate the steps that precede the commercial-readiness timeline. (See Exhibit 3.) Operators adopting IMSaaS need not independently source and coordinate IMS software, infrastructure, and integration services, a task that often extends across multiple vendors. Instead, they procure a pre-integrated managed service from a single accountable service provider, thereby reducing technical evaluation and contractual complexity and significantly shortening sourcing and contracting compared with the operator-deployed model.

Following this speedier sourcing and contracting process, actual implementation accelerates. too. Moving from traditional IMS to operator-deployed cloud-native IMS reduces time to commercial readiness by approximately 50%, primarily through shorter design cycles, automated testing, and reusable test environments. IMSaaS builds on these benefits through standardized service designs and reusable integration assets, reducing implementation time by an additional 30% or so. Although telcos can provision standardized IMS software within minutes, operator-specific network integration, testing, and certification take longer and remain necessary before commercial readiness.Another CNaaS benefit is more repeatable delivery with materially lower operator-side effort and capability requirements. Standardized designs and reusable integration assets reduce one-off design and implementation effort. Similarly, shared specialist operations, monitoring, and life-cycle management reduce the need for operators to build and maintain dedicated platform tooling and specialist capabilities.Total Cost of Ownership Declines
By lowering hardware and operating costs, the operator-deployed cloud-native IMS model significantly lowers TCO compared with the traditional IMS model, which relies on peak-load sizing, large capacity increments, active/standby reserves, and a larger number of manual life-cycle operations. (See Exhibit 4.) The smaller hardware footprint becomes increasingly valuable as memory and broader server costs rise.

IMSaaS adds benefits by standardizing and sharing platform architecture, integration capabilities, monitoring and automation, specialist operations, and life-cycle management across deployments. These features reduce the dedicated fixed costs and capabilities that each operator would otherwise need to build and maintain. The advantages are most pronounced with a smaller subscriber base. For 1 million subscribers, the annualized five-year TCO per subscriber is approximately 50% lower than for an operator-deployed cloud-native IMS and 80% lower than traditional IMS.But the relative IMSaaS advantage shrinks as the IMS subscriber base broadens. An operator-deployed cloud-native IMS can spread its upfront build, integration. and hardware costs across a larger subscriber base; benefit from licensing discounts at scale; and reduce the operating resources required per subscriber. This cuts the IMSaaS advantage from approximately 50% for 1 million subscribers to approximately 10% for 5 million subscribers.Industrializing Cloud-Native Network Services
The strategic question for most operators is no longer whether to adopt cloud-native networks, but rather which network capabilities to build and operate internally and which to source through a standardized, shared-service model. As our IMS case study shows, CNaaS is most attractive where standardization and reuse are high and when dedicated internal capabilities are difficult to justify given the scale of the service or use case. Operator-deployed solutions remain attractive when it is necessary to maintain direct control over established service scale, customization, sovereignty, and regulatory requirements.CNaaS offers operators of all sizes an alternative to building and operating dedicated core network capabilities in-house. Applications range from IMS, IoT core, MVNO, and mobile virtual network enabler services to core capabilities supporting private enterprise networks, NTN connectivity, and roaming. Beyond these applications, emerging commercial offerings and initial deployments demonstrate how CNaaS is extending toward more comprehensive, turnkey mobile core solutions that support enhanced mobile broadband.BCG would like to thank Orange Wholesale and ng-voice for providing data and for sharing insights from their experience, which informed the IMSaaS analysis in this paper.
